name: A separate guard model is a second LLM in the request path, and its cost is bounded below by seconds - not by the size of the flag you set
symptom: Expectation is that 'add Llama Guard' is a policy toggle. Reality is a model forward pass on every request, and even the smallest published guard (Llama Guard 3-1B-INT4, 440 MB, about 7x smaller than the fp 1B) reports TTFT of 2.5 s or less and at least 30 tok/s on a commodity Android mobile CPU. Co-located on a GPU with the main model it is far cheaper than that, but it is neither free nor automatically parallel with the main generation.
root_cause: A guard model is a second autoregressive forward pass. Llama Guard's design applies one taxonomy-bearing model to BOTH the prompt and the response, so a fully guarded conversation can incur two guard passes per turn, not one. Cost depends on the model chosen: ShieldGemma reports +10.8% AU-PRC over Llama Guard and +4.3% over WildCard on public benchmarks, so accuracy and cost trade against each other with published numbers rather than being a free upgrade.
workaround: Budget the guard pass as a latency line item and measure it rather than assuming it. Quantise it. If you can only afford one guarded turn, guard the response - where the harmful content actually is - rather than doubling up on the prompt. Do not treat a guard as a substitute for in-decode masking when the threat model includes adaptive jailbreaks: JailbreakBench tracks attacks AND defences, and both layers are needed.
notes: Self-Guard's framing is the useful summary of the whole field: safety training cannot adapt to new attack types and drops performance, while safeguards (external models or filters) have been of limited help. Neither family is a control you can rely on alone. Residual risk is over-refusal, which JailbreakBench measures with a dedicated over-refusal dataset - a guard that refuses everything scores well on harmfulness and badly on usefulness.
